common_name: White Clockvine (White Lady, Sweet Clockvine, Fragrant Thunbergia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines or rooted cuttings in spring on a light trellis, fence, or arbor in full sun to partial shade; White Clockvine spreads readily by seed and runners in zone 9-11, so site it where volunteer seedlings can be managed or deadhead promptly to limit self-sowing.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; White Clockvine is a fast, twining perennial vine from South and Southeast Asia that bears star-shaped, pure white flowers with a soft yellow throat, each about 1.5-2 inches across, held above the foliage rather than dangling like many other Thunbergia species. It blooms nearly continuously in warm weather and tolerates both humid Gulf Coast summers and brief dry spells once established. In zone 9a it dies back hard after frost but returns reliably from the roots each spring; in zone 10-11 it is evergreen and can naturalize aggressively, so gardeners in frost-free areas should monitor and contain its spread away from natural areas. Light, twiggy support such as a mailbox post, low fence, or shrub is sufficient since it is less rampant than Bengal clockvine.

common_name: Laurel Clockvine (Blue Trumpet Vine, Rang Jeud)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring on a very sturdy pergola, arbor, or fence in full sun; Laurel Clockvine grows extremely vigorously in warm humid summers and needs a large, permanent structure to support its long twining stems.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade on a sturdy, permanent support; Laurel Clockvine is a vigorous twining vine native from India through Indochina to Malaysia, producing pendulous racemes of lavender-blue to violet trumpet-shaped flowers with a pale yellow throat, each bloom 3-4 inches across. It is closely related to and often confused with Bengal Clockvine (T. grandiflora) but is distinguished by smooth, entire leaf margins rather than shallow-lobed leaves, and by a somewhat softer lavender-blue flower color. In zone 9a it typically freezes back to the roots in winter and resprouts vigorously in spring; in zone 10-11 it is evergreen and blooms nearly year-round. Because it spreads by both root suckers and stem fragments, confine it to areas where its growth can be controlled and kept away from natural waterways.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring on a sturdy pergola or arbor in full sun with some protection from harsh midday heat; Scarlet Clockvine is a vigorous woody climber best sited where its long pendulous flower clusters can hang freely and be viewed from below.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade with some relief from intense afternoon heat; Scarlet Clockvine is a vigorous, woody twining vine native to the Himalayan foothills through Indochina and southern China, producing long, cascading racemes of tubular flowers that range from deep scarlet to burnt orange-red, set against large, heart-shaped, soft green leaves. Unlike the blue- and violet-flowered Thunbergia species, its warm red-orange coloring and hanging clusters make it a strong hummingbird and butterfly attractant through the warm months. It grows best trained onto a large pergola or arbor where the pendant flower clusters can dangle freely for viewing from below. In zone 9a it dies back to the roots after frost and resprouts in spring; in zone 10-11 it is evergreen and blooms over a longer season. Provide consistent moisture during active growth but avoid waterlogged soil.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost or purchase transplants; set out in hanging baskets, containers, or at the base of a small trellis after all danger of frost has passed. In zones 9-11 it behaves as a tender perennial and can be planted directly in spring.

directions: Grow in containers, hanging baskets, or at the base of a small trellis in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Blushing Susie' is a warm-toned selection of black-eyed Susan vine that opens in soft apricot and peach shades and deepens through rose, red, and cream tones as each bloom ages, so a single plant displays several colors at once. Its trailing, twining habit and continuous summer-into-fall bloom make it especially suited to hanging baskets and mixed containers, where stems can cascade freely or be trained up a small obelisk. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and a fuller display, and feed lightly through the growing season to sustain continuous flowering. It performs reliably in Gulf Coast humidity and tolerates part shade better than most flowering annual vines.

common_name: Arizona Dark Red Black-Eyed Susan Vine

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost or purchase transplants; set out after all danger of frost has passed on a trellis, obelisk, or in a hanging basket. In zones 9-11 it grows as a tender perennial and can be direct sown or planted in spring.

directions: Grow on a trellis, obelisk, or in a large hanging basket in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Arizona Dark Red' is a compact, floriferous selection from the Arizona Series bred for uniform, deep brick-red to bronze-red flowers with the classic dark central eye, blooming heavily from early summer through frost. It branches more freely than seed-grown mixes, producing a denser cover of flowers along the twining stems, and its shorter internodes make it well suited to smaller trellises and mixed containers as well as full-size garden supports. Pinch young vines at planting to promote branching, and provide even moisture through summer heat to keep flower production continuous. It tolerates the humidity and heat of Gulf Coast summers well and attracts hummingbirds and butterflies.
